Prop
3
CA
Prop
3
|
Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Prop. 98 requires California to provide a minimum level of funding for K–12 schools and community colleges each year, based on state revenues, economic growth, and student enrollment. Local property taxes also contribute to the Prop. 98 minimum. Together, these requirements typically direct about 40% of General Fund revenues to education. 3
Of the education funding, 89% goes to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. None of the funding can be used for administrative costs. After meeting education requirements, revenues go to debt service and the rainy day fund; 50% of remaining funds, capped at $2 billion annually, may support Medi-Cal children’s and family health services.
Medi-Cal provides free or low-cost health care to nearly 15 million Californians. This funding is especially important after federal bill H.R. 1 made major cuts to health care and food assistance. Federal Medicaid cuts could cost Medi-Cal tens of billions of dollars annually and cause up to 2 million Californians to lose coverage.
Since January 1, 2012, the top-earner income tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, helping more than double school funding and support transitional kindergarten, expanded learning, free school meals, COVID-19 recovery, and teacher recruitment. 4 Before the passage of Prop. 30, California ranked 50th among states in per-student education spending. Now it ranks 16th (or 31st when accounting for the state’s cost of living). 5 However, because 80% of school spending goes to staff salaries and benefits, the state still has 22 students per teacher, compared with 15.4 nationally. 6
Recently, the tax has generated about $9 billion to $10 billion annually, although revenues fluctuate with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates annual revenues could range from $5 billion to $15 billion.
Notably, high earners have not fled the state because of this tax; California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade. 7 The state has lost less-educated and lower-income adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults because of affordability and cost-of-living concerns. 8
Californians for Protecting Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability led the effort to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, with funding from the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers. Some proponents oppose Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax, out of concern that it could undermine support for Prop. 3.
A citizen-initiated measure, Prop. 3 needs a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Allowing the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to expire would require major cuts to education spending on the next generation of Californians, which would disproportionately impact low-income children and students of color. This income tax revenue enabled California to become the first state offering free breakfast and lunch to all TK–12 students, plus free after-school programs prioritizing low-income neighborhoods.
California’s educational funding formula, the Local Control Funding Formula, directs the most resources to students who face the greatest educational hurdles, including grants for English learners, foster youth, homeless students, and low-income families in high-poverty districts. 9
Prop. 3 would backfill federal cuts and sustain up to $2 billion in annual funding for Medi-Cal, most of which goes to low-income people and people of color. Without state budget and policy intervention, the cuts from H.R. 1 are expected to completely destabilize California’s healthcare and hospital system, exacerbate food insecurity, and cause children to miss routine screenings and vaccines. 10
The measure is highly progressive; it does not increase taxes on couples earning less than $743,001 or individuals earning less than $341,001, in today’s dollars.
Pros
Prop. 3 would help backfill ongoing funding needs for children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal, which is facing severe federal funding cuts.
The measure would tax only California’s highest earners.
It would not increase the current income tax rate, which was set in 2012.
Any leftover capital-gains-driven revenue would lower state debt and help build the rainy day fund, which supports the state’s financial health and mitigates the volatility of this funding source.
There is no evidence that the tax has contributed to any significant tax flight from the state.
Because the tax is permanent, it would facilitate greater predictability in state revenues.
Cons
The state’s reliance on taxing the highest income earners would increase state budget volatility.
The measure is restrictive: it would require meeting the Prop. 98 education minimum before allowing flexibility in funding allocation.
Vote YES

Should Voters Approve Prop. 3? How Top Tax Rates Have Helped Californians
A Look at What California's Top Tax Rates Have Funded — and What's at Risk if Voters Don't Approve Prop. 3
July 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 3 will appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot, asking California voters whether to make permanent the higher-income tax rates on the state’s highest earners. These top tax rates were first enacted by voters in 2012 and renewed in 2016 to help fund schools, health care, and other supports for working families. Without action, the current rates are set to expire after 2030, reducing state revenues by billions of dollars annually and threatening funding for schools and state programs and services that support Californians every day.
table of Contents
What Would Prop. 3 Do?
Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55
Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?
Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Credit
Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared
What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?
Why Renewing the Top Tax Rates Matters for California
What Would Prop. 3 Do?
Prop. 3 would make permanent the rates put in place since 2012, preserving a key element of progressivity (requiring households with higher incomes to pay higher tax rates) in the state’s revenue structure that funds critical investments that improve the quality of life for all Californians. The measure would not raise taxes or change existing income tax rates; it simply removes the expiration date on current tax rates for the state’s highest earners. Revenues would continue to support the entire state General Fund budget by helping meet the TK-14 constitutional funding guarantee and freeing up revenue for other programs and services, just as they have since 2012.
Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55
In 2012, after the state faced significant revenue losses as a result of the Great Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which added new income tax brackets for the state’s highest earners (10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3%, depending on household income) and included a temporary sales tax increase. Both the income tax rates and the sales tax increase were temporary, with the sales tax set to expire in 2016 and the income tax rates in 2018. Proposition 30 also created the Education Protection Account, a state account in the General Fund that receives and disburses revenues from the top income tax rates.
what is the education protection account (epa)?
Proposition 30 (2012) established the Education Protection Account, a state account where revenues from the top income tax rates are deposited. Of the funds in the account, 89% are distributed to schools and 11% to community colleges. This revenue is treated as General Fund revenue, subject to constitutional requirements including Prop. 98 (1988), the state’s minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education, and Prop. 2 (2014), which established rules for building state budget reserves and paying down state debts. The revenue deposited into the EPA increases the Prop. 98 guarantee and is used to help meet the guarantee, freeing up General Fund revenue for other state budget priorities.
In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended the income tax rates for another 12 years (to 2030), while allowing the sales tax to expire as scheduled. Prop. 55 also added a constitutional formula intended to increase funding for the Medi-Cal program (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3765) when revenues exceed a certain threshold. This specific formula has never directed funds to Medi-Cal, and the current measure would allow it to expire. However, top tax rate revenues do support the Medi-Cal budget indirectly through the General Fund capacity generated by Prop. 55.
Since their initial enactment in 2012, these higher tax rates have generated around $120 billion for schools and other essential services. In recent years, the higher rates have generated around $10 billion annually. These revenues now form a core component of the state budget, supporting the TK-14 education budget, strengthening General Fund capacity to support other vital programs and services, and building reserves.
Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?
The voter-approved top tax rates only impact the highest-income Californians.
These rates only apply to the top 2% of California tax filers (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016). In tax year 2025, these top rates only applied to people with incomes above around $371,000 for single tax filers and about $743,000 for married couples filing jointly. These thresholds increase annually with inflation.
Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Cut
The top-earning 1% of Californians would receive a major tax cut if Prop. 55 rates are not extended. If the voter-approved top tax rates are allowed to expire, the vast majority of tax filers in the top 1% by income would receive an average annual tax cut of nearly $59,000, according to estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. This top 1% group would get about 98% of the total tax cuts. The remaining tax cuts would go to some households in the next 4% of highest-income filers. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Not all households in the top 5% or top 1% would receive tax cuts from the expiration of the top tax rates for several reasons. First, filers are subject to the top tax rates if their taxable income — that is, income after accounting for allowed exemptions and deductions — exceeds the thresholds established by Prop. 30 and Prop. 50. In contrast, the thresholds for the top 5% and top 1% used by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for this analysis are based on total income before exemptions and deductions. So tax filers in the top 1% by total income may have taxable incomes under the threshold for the top rates. Second, some high-income filers that use specific tax preferences may be subject to an “alternative minimum tax,” which could be triggered if their regular tax bill were reduced. And finally, because thresholds for these rates vary by household type, a married couple filing a joint tax return with a total income of $500,000 falls into the top 5% of all tax filers, but their total income — even before accounting for exemptions and deductions — is below the threshold for the Prop. 55 taxes of around $743,000, for example. Around 15% of this group would receive a tax cut, averaging more than $2,000 annually. Californians in all other income groups would see no change to their taxes.
California’s tax system would be more regressive if the Prop. 55 tax rates expire. A regressive tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/) is one in which lower-income households pay larger shares of their income in taxes than higher-income households. In contrast, in a progressive tax system, higher-income people pay higher shares of their income in taxes. California’s tax system is more progressive than many other state tax systems (https://itep.org/whopays-7th-edition/), in large part due to these voter-approved top tax rates that are up for renewal under Prop. 3.
When you add up the various state and local taxes that Californians pay — including the sales tax, property tax, and other types of taxes — the highest-income 1% currently pay about 12% of their income in taxes on average. That’s barely more than the 11.7% paid by Californians in the lowest 20% by income. If the top rates were not in effect, the top 1% would pay only about 10.7% of their income in state and local taxes — lower than what the bottom fifth of Californians pay.
Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared
The number of Californians with incomes high enough to be subject to the voter-approved top tax rates has more than doubled, reflecting soaring incomes among top earners. Around 185,000 tax filers, including more than 175,000 California resident filers, had incomes above the thresholds for Prop. 30’s top tax rates in 2013, the first year the rates were in effect. By 2024 (the latest available data), the number had reached nearly 376,000, including around 355,000 California residents. 2 (javascript:void(0)) “Tax filer” represents a tax filing unit — the primary filer as well as any spouses and dependents included on the tax return. A tax filing unit can be an individual, a couple, or a family, and in some cases can include unrelated dependents. This increase is due to the incomes of these high-income households growing much faster than inflation over this period.
Californians subject to the top tax rates have seen their incomes grow dramatically over the past several decades, while most Californians have lost ground or experienced income declines after adjusting for inflation . The top 1% of Californians saw their inflation-adjusted incomes increase more than 2.5 times (157%) between 1987 and 2024, while those in the bottom 80% saw decreases in real income over that time.
To be in the top 1%, a tax filer had an income of at least $973,097 in 2024. On average, this group reported more than $3 million per tax return in 2024 — about 54 times the income of the middle fifth of Californians, who earned around $56,000 on average. In even starker contrast, the top 0.1% had an average income of over $15 million — 268 times that of the middle fifth of Californians. In other words, someone in the top 1% can earn in just under one week what the average middle-income Californian earns in an entire year, and someone in the top 0.1% can earn that amount in just over a day .
What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?
Since the passage of Prop. 30 in 2012, the top tax rates have generated about $120 billion in state revenue. 3 (javascript:void(0)) This figure reflects revenues from the top tax rates allocated to TK-14 education from the Education Protection Account (EPA) through the 2024-25 fiscal year. On average, this revenue has represented about 5.5% of total General Fund revenues. The funds raised by the top tax rates approved by voters through Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have been a major revenue source for the state, supporting critical services including education, health care, and economic security programs. This revenue has also helped the state to build up budget reserves to be better prepared for downturns when revenues decline or come in lower than expected.
The annual revenue raised by the top tax rates has increased in line with overall state revenues . These revenues are sensitive to stock market fluctuations, as a large share of the income of high-income households comes from earnings on investments such as dividends and capital gains. For example, Prop. 55 revenues peaked at more than $16 billion when the stock market surged in 2021 and then subsequently fell in line with the stock market decline in the following years, before growing to nearly $12 billion in 2024. The sensitivity of these revenues to economic conditions makes it all the more important that state leaders have the capacity to save revenues during high-revenue years in the state’s budget reserves for future downturns, as required under Prop. 2 of 2014 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/140924_Proposition_2_BB.pdf)— which may be modified to require additional savings in some strong-revenue years if voters approve changes to the existing measure with Prop. 2 on the November 2026 ballot.
Top tax rate revenues provide critical support for schools and community colleges . Top tax rate revenues serve two purposes for the TK-14 education budget: 1) increase the Prop. 98 minimum guarantee’s annual calculation and 2) provide the revenues needed to meet the guarantee. Because top tax rate revenues count as General Fund revenues, they directly affect how the annual Prop. 98 level is calculated. The new issue of the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* is out and it contains a study by economists Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu titled “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California.”
Back in 2019, I wrote about an earlier version of this study that examined “the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income”:
> In 2012, Californians facing “temporary” multi-billion dollar budget deficits passed Proposition 30.
This included a 3.45% sales tax increase as well as a $42 billion “temporary” increase in the state’s progressive income tax rates.
Rauh and Shyu find that wealthy Californians were about 40% more likely to leave after the income tax hike, mostly to states without income taxes.
They also found that these departures and other responses to increased taxes eliminated 45.2% of the revenue the state expected to get from high earners.
Within two years, 60.9% of this windfall had been eroded.
It turns out that there are limits to taxing the rich, even in a state like California with all the advantages of climate and the like which it has.

| | | |# Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California *Joshua Rauh* and *Ryan Shyu* *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy*, 2024, vol. 16, issue 1, 34-86 **Abstract:** Using administrative data, we analyze the response to Proposition 30, a 2012 measure that increased California marginal tax rates by up to 3 percentage points for high-income households.
Relative to baseline departure rates, an additional 0.8 percent of the residential tax base that landed in the top bracket left California in 2013.

4. Accountability provisions: EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs; annual audits; criminal penalties for misuse; districts post accounting online. Local boards decide spending.
5. 3. Entrenches revenue volatility: half of state income tax from top 2%, tied to capital gains/stock market; Prop 98 minimum guarantee linked to volatile revenue → boom/bust cycles in school funding. LAO and Chronicle both flag this.
4. November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by
making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.
Advertisement
Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.
Advertisement
Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”

Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.

Very useful. Key new info:
- LA Times' George Skelton recommends NO (constitutional entrenchment argument: "Tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters... And there's no rush. The rates don't expire for five years.").
- LA Times news piece: "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" — about 40% to education, 60% to other general fund programs. This is a fact-check that the campaign's framing overstates the school share.
- Rauh & Shyu 2024: significant behavioral responses eroded 45-61% of windfall revenue, mostly intensive margin (income shifting, reduced income generation), 0.8pp increased outmigration. Note: This matters for the LAO's $5-15B estimate — the LAO estimate is based on the current revenue actually collected under those rates (which already reflects behavioral responses, since these rates have been in place since 2012). So making them permanent doesn't change rates; the "erosion" already happened. Important nuance: Rauh & Shyu's estimate pertains to a rate change (increase). Prop 3 doesn't change the rates — it just prevents a future decrease. If the rates fall in 2031, would income come back? Possibly partially, plus people who left might return. So the LAO's $5-15B may overstate the revenue that would actually be lost if rates expire... Actually, the LAO's estimate for the loss is likely based on current revenue from those brackets, which is real revenue actually collected now ($10-12B recently). So it's the actual current revenue. But there's an argument that a rate reduction could produce more revenue than the naive "windfall" symmetry implies — i.e., some income might come back. Conversely, if rates stay, there could be continued erosion over time. The LAO range of $5-15B accounts for volatility.

Let me now check the LA Times article "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" for the detail, plus the LAO's earlier initiative analysis (A.G. File 2025-016) for more nuance, and any analysis of what happens if it fails (whether the Legislature would replace it). Also, check campaign finance: how much was raised/spent on both sides (the no side appears underfunded).

Also I should consider the counterfactual: if Prop 3 fails, does the Legislature have to do something? Rates expire in 2031; the Legislature could act with a 2/3 vote, or voters could pass something in 2028/2030. So a "no" vote is not necessarily a permanent loss of revenue — but it creates a cliff and uncertainty, and the political economy makes restoration hard (a 2/3 legislative vote is unlikely; a future ballot measure is possible but not guaranteed).

Let me also consider: is there something problematic about the measure's drafting? E.g., it amends Article XIII Section 36 in full text — which also includes the 2011 realignment provisions. Also, the Medi-Cal formula in Prop 55 (subparagraph F) — the measure keeps it (50% of remainder up to $2B). Also, does Prop 3 remove the "Public School System Stabilization Account" provisions? No, it amends Section 36(e)(2) to remove the 2030 date limits presumably. Let me check the remaining text (offset 40000) to see the last part and any other amendments (e.g., whether the sunset removals are properly drafted, and whether Section 7 proponent standing etc.).

Actually, an important drafting question: does the measure delete the "inoperative on December 1, 2031" clauses? The text shown includes "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." — Wait, that appears in the text I fetched. Hmm, but the strikeout/italic formatting is lost in the plain text extraction. The LAO says Prop 3 removes the sunset. In the printed VIG, deleted text is in strikeout. The plain-text extraction shows both deleted and added text without formatting. So "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." is likely in strikeout (deleted). Let me verify with the LAO analysis PDF (lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) which includes Figure 1 and describes the proposal.

Let me also check the remaining chunk of the text (offset 40000) to see if there's anything else notable.

Then I'll consider the final decision. Let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
1. Not a new tax — maintains rates in place 15 years; avoids an abrupt $5-15B annual revenue cliff (2-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031.
2. Revenue supports Prop 98 education minimum and frees General Fund for Medi-Cal (facing federal cuts under H.R. 1), reserves, debt paydown.
3. Highly progressive: top 1% gets 98% of the tax cut if it expires (ITEP). Without the rates, the top 1% would pay a lower effective state/local tax share than the bottom 20% (per CBPC).
4. Accountability provisions: EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs; annual audits; criminal penalties for misuse; districts post accounting online. Local boards decide spending.
5. Migration evidence is mixed/weak: FTB measured outmigration at 0.1-0.2% of those subject to higher rate; CA has second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves; Young & Varner found near-zero millionaire migration elasticity.
6. Broad, mainstream support: CTA, PTA, school nurses, CMA (doctors), firefighters, Planned Parenthood, Cal Dem Party, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, SPUR, LA Times (no official board position but coverage). Polling shows ~54-58% support.
7. The alternative — a no vote — doesn't produce reform; it just risks a cliff. The "message vote" theory has a poor track record (Prop 55 in 2016 got rejected by Chronicle board expecting reform; none happened).

Arguments for NO:
1. "Temporary" becomes permanent — a broken promise; sets precedent.
2. Entrenches rates and earmarks in the Constitution, removing legislative flexibility; tax rates in the constitution can only be changed by voters (Skelton's point). Locks in Prop 98 + EPA earmark structure; makes comprehensive tax reform harder (e.g., broadening the base, reducing volatility).
3. Entrenches revenue volatility: half of state income tax from top 2%, tied to capital gains/stock market; Prop 98 minimum guarantee linked to volatile revenue → boom/bust cycles in school funding. LAO and Chronicle both flag this.
4. Behavioral responses: Rauh & Shyu find significant intensive-margin erosion; making the high rates permanent could increase incentives for long-run income shifting, and interacts with Prop 40 wealth tax and other measures (software tax, health insurance tax) raising the cumulative tax burden → competitiveness concerns; top rate 13.3% is highest in nation.
5. Cost-of-living/political-economy: 55% of Californians prefer lower taxes/fewer services; small-business pass-through burden (NFIB).
6. No reform attached: measure has no spending accountability for the ~60% that goes to non-education General Fund uses, despite campaign claims that "every dollar goes to schools." The LA Times fact-check shows the campaign framing overstates. Also, no education-outcome accountability (SDUT argument: spending up, outcomes flat).
7. There's time: rates don't expire until 2031; the Legislature/voters could revisit in 2028 or 2030 with reforms attached (e.g., a broadened base, spending reforms). A no vote creates leverage.

Counter to the "no rush" point: the campaign needs to happen well in advance of 2031 for budget planning; also CTA put it on the ballot now for a reason (midterm electorate more favorable? Actually, midterms are usually worse for tax measures — low turnout, more conservative electorate. Hmm, but polls show it passing).

Consider the risk asymmetry: If Prop 3 passes and later turns out that reform was needed, the rates can still be changed by a future ballot measure (majority vote) — the constitution can be amended by initiative. So permanence isn't irreversible: it just requires a ballot measure rather than a 2/3 legislative vote. That reduces the "lock-in" concern significantly. Indeed, if a majority of voters later wanted lower rates, they could pass an initiative to lower them (though initiative to lower taxes is straightforward—statutory or constitutional). So permanence is a moderate, not extreme, loss of flexibility.

If Prop 3 fails: a $5-15B hole (midpoint ~$10B, ~4% of General Fund) appears in 2031-32, requiring either deep cuts to schools/health care or a new tax measure or 2/3 legislative action (unlikely in the current political climate, and even more unlikely given anti-tax momentum). Also uncertainty harms multi-year budget planning, and the state currently faces structural deficits. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) starting to bite, and CA's structural deficit, losing $10B/year would force real cuts. CTA claims 15% school budget cut; that's probably overstated (the LAO says ~40% goes to education, so a $10B loss → ~$4-6B less for schools; Prop 98 guarantee would fall accordingly). Still significant.

Given the framing "yes or no" and my analysis, the balance favors YES: it maintains existing, broadly popular, highly progressive revenue; avoids a large fiscal cliff; includes real accountability provisions; the migration evidence is mixed and mostly points to modest effects; and the loss of flexibility is bounded because a future initiative can still change rates. The strongest counterarguments (entrenchment of volatility, broken "temporary" promise, no structural reform) are real but are second-order compared with a $5-15B annual revenue cliff during a period of federal health care cuts.

Let me do a couple more checks to be thorough:
- LAO PDF Figure 1 & proposal description (confirm sunset removal, and whether Prop 55's Medi-Cal formula is retained or allowed to expire).
- Campaign finance totals for both sides.
- Any notable "no" endorsements from unusual quarters (e.g., some Democrats like Gov. Newsom? Reform California? Also, does any progressive group oppose on grounds it forecloses a better deal?).
- Check the LA Times fact-check article details.

But there's an argument that a rate reduction could produce more revenue than the naive "windfall" symmetry implies — i.e., some income might come back. Conversely, if rates stay, there could be continued erosion over time. The LAO range of $5-15B accounts for volatility.

Let me now check the LA Times article "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" for the detail, plus the LAO's earlier initiative analysis (A.G. File 2025-016) for more nuance, and any analysis of what happens if it fails (whether the Legislature would replace it). Also, check campaign finance: how much was raised/spent on both sides (the no side appears underfunded).

Also I should consider the counterfactual: if Prop 3 fails, does the Legislature have to do something? Rates expire in 2031; the Legislature could act with a 2/3 vote, or voters could pass something in 2028/2030. So a "no" vote is not necessarily a permanent loss of revenue — but it creates a cliff and uncertainty, and the political economy makes restoration hard (a 2/3 legislative vote is unlikely; a future ballot measure is possible but not guaranteed).

Let me also consider: is there something problematic about the measure's drafting? E.g., it amends Article XIII Section 36 in full text — which also includes the 2011 realignment provisions. Also, the Medi-Cal formula in Prop 55 (subparagraph F) — the measure keeps it (50% of remainder up to $2B). Also, does Prop 3 remove the "Public School System Stabilization Account" provisions? No, it amends Section 36(e)(2) to remove the 2030 date limits presumably. Let me check the remaining text (offset 40000) to see the last part and any other amendments (e.g., whether the sunset removals are properly drafted, and whether Section 7 proponent standing etc.).

Actually, an important drafting question: does the measure delete the "inoperative on December 1, 2031" clauses? The text shown includes "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." — Wait, that appears in the text I fetched. Hmm, but the strikeout/italic formatting is lost in the plain text extraction. The LAO says Prop 3 removes the sunset. In the printed VIG, deleted text is in strikeout. The plain-text extraction shows both deleted and added text without formatting. So "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." is likely in strikeout (deleted). Let me verify with the LAO analysis PDF (lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) which includes Figure 1 and describes the proposal.

Let me also check the remaining chunk of the text (offset 40000) to see if there's anything else notable.

Then I'll consider the final decision. Let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
1. Not a new tax — maintains rates in place 15 years; avoids an abrupt $5-15B annual revenue cliff (2-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031.
2. Revenue supports Prop 98 education minimum and frees General Fund for Medi-Cal (facing federal cuts under H.R. 1), reserves, debt paydown.
3. Highly progressive: top 1% gets 98% of the tax cut if it expires (ITEP). Without the rates, the top 1% would pay a lower effective state/local tax share than the bottom 20% (per CBPC).
4. Accountability provisions: EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs; annual audits; criminal penalties for misuse; districts post accounting online. Local boards decide spending.
5. Migration evidence is mixed/weak: FTB measured outmigration at 0.1-0.2% of those subject to higher rate; CA has second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves; Young & Varner found near-zero millionaire migration elasticity.
6. Broad, mainstream support: CTA, PTA, school nurses, CMA (doctors), firefighters, Planned Parenthood, Cal Dem Party, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, SPUR, LA Times (no official board position but coverage). Polling shows ~54-58% support.
7. The alternative — a no vote — doesn't produce reform; it just risks a cliff. The "message vote" theory has a poor track record (Prop 55 in 2016 got rejected by Chronicle board expecting reform; none happened).

Arguments for NO:
1. "Temporary" becomes permanent — a broken promise; sets precedent.
2. Entrenches rates and earmarks in the Constitution, removing legislative flexibility; tax rates in the constitution can only be changed by voters (Skelton's point). Locks in Prop 98 + EPA earmark structure; makes comprehensive tax reform harder (e.g., broadening the base, reducing volatility).
3. Entrenches revenue volatility: half of state income tax from top 2%, tied to capital gains/stock market; Prop 98 minimum guarantee linked to volatile revenue → boom/bust cycles in school funding. LAO and Chronicle both flag this.
4. Behavioral responses: Rauh & Shyu find significant intensive-margin erosion; making the high rates permanent could increase incentives for long-run income shifting, and interacts with Prop 40 wealth tax and other measures (software tax, health insurance tax) raising the cumulative tax burden → competitiveness concerns; top rate 13.3% is highest in nation.
5. Cost-of-living/political-economy: 55% of Californians prefer lower taxes/fewer services; small-business pass-through burden (NFIB).
6. No reform attached: measure has no spending accountability for the ~60% that goes to non-education General Fund uses, despite campaign claims that "every dollar goes to schools." The LA Times fact-check shows the campaign framing overstates. Also, no education-outcome accountability (SDUT argument: spending up, outcomes flat).
7. There's time: rates don't expire until 2031; the Legislature/voters could revisit in 2028 or 2030 with reforms attached (e.g., a broadened base, spending reforms). A no vote creates leverage.

Counter to the "no rush" point: the campaign needs to happen well in advance of 2031 for budget planning; also CTA put it on the ballot now for a reason (midterm electorate more favorable? Actually, midterms are usually worse for tax measures — low turnout, more conservative electorate. Hmm, but polls show it passing).

Consider the risk asymmetry: If Prop 3 passes and later turns out that reform was needed, the rates can still be changed by a future ballot measure (majority vote) — the constitution can be amended by initiative. So permanence isn't irreversible: it just requires a ballot measure rather than a 2/3 legislative vote. That reduces the "lock-in" concern significantly. Indeed, if a majority of voters later wanted lower rates, they could pass an initiative to lower them (though initiative to lower taxes is straightforward—statutory or constitutional). So permanence is a moderate, not extreme, loss of flexibility.

If Prop 3 fails: a $5-15B hole (midpoint ~$10B, ~4% of General Fund) appears in 2031-32, requiring either deep cuts to schools/health care or a new tax measure or 2/3 legislative action (unlikely in the current political climate, and even more unlikely given anti-tax momentum). Also uncertainty harms multi-year budget planning, and the state currently faces structural deficits. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) starting to bite, and CA's structural deficit, losing $10B/year would force real cuts. CTA claims 15% school budget cut; that's probably overstated (the LAO says ~40% goes to education, so a $10B loss → ~$4-6B less for schools; Prop 98 guarantee would fall accordingly). Still significant.

Given the framing "yes or no" and my analysis, the balance favors YES: it maintains existing, broadly popular, highly progressive revenue; avoids a large fiscal cliff; includes real accountability provisions; the migration evidence is mixed and mostly points to modest effects; and the loss of flexibility is bounded because a future initiative can still change rates. The strongest counterarguments (entrenchment of volatility, broken "temporary" promise, no structural reform) are real but are second-order compared with a $5-15B annual revenue cliff during a period of federal health care cuts.

Let me do a couple more checks to be thorough:
- LAO PDF Figure 1 & proposal description (confirm sunset removal, and whether Prop 55's Medi-Cal formula is retained or allowed to expire).
- Campaign finance totals for both sides.
- Any notable "no" endorsements from unusual quarters (e.g., some Democrats like Gov. Newsom? Reform California? Also, does any progressive group oppose on grounds it forecloses a better deal?).
- Check the LA Times fact-check article details.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by
making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.

In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.

Very useful. Key facts:
- CTA spent ~$60M; total $81M for, $5,500 against (essentially no opposition campaign).
- Some billionaires (Building a Better California) endorse Prop 3 while fighting Prop 40.
- Gov. Newsom supports Prop 3 (per LA Times: "Others in that camp include ... Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra" — that camp being Yes on 3 and No on 40).

Let me now check a couple more things:
1. Any credible criticism from the left or good-government groups (e.g., League of Women Voters California position; Common Cause; California Forward).
2. What the LAO said in its initiative analysis (A.G. File 2025-016) — including any unusual notes, e.g., whether the measure would prevent the Legislature from changing rates (2/3 requirement is already needed for tax increases; but rate decreases could be done by majority? Actually under Prop 30/55 constitutional provisions, the rates are in the constitution, so amending requires 2/3 legislative or initiative. Under Prop 3 the same). Note: Under current law the rates already can't be changed without a ballot measure/2/3 legislative vote (since they're in the constitution). So making them permanent doesn't reduce flexibility much compared to now — the Legislature could amend the constitutional provisions with a 2/3 vote to let them sunset earlier or change rates. Wait, that's an important nuance: Article XIII Section 36(e)(f) is constitutional; the Legislature can amend a voter-approved constitutional provision only with 2/3 and voter approval. So the rates are already effectively locked in the constitution until 2030. Prop 3 removes the sunset. So future change requires either 2/3 legislature + majority voters, or an initiative. This is the same as today, just with a later date. So Skelton's concern ("tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters") is already true — they're embedded now. Prop 3 just extends the embedding indefinitely. So the incremental loss of flexibility is modest: currently, the sunset provides an automatic "release valve" in 2031 — voting no preserves that release valve.

That's actually the crux: the automatic expiration in 2031 is the one leverage point that forces the Legislature to engage in tax reform negotiation. If Prop 3 passes, that pressure disappears, and the status quo (volatile, top-heavy income tax + Prop 98 earmark) becomes permanent absent a future initiative.

3. Also check the state's structural deficit situation for 2026-27, LAO's fiscal outlook, to gauge the stakes. And whether a "no" vote would create a crisis in 2031 or whether the state could offset.

4. Check League of Women Voters California position and any other nonpartisan guides (e.g., California Forward, Silicon Valley Leadership Group).

Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers.

File 2025-016) — including any unusual notes, e.g., whether the measure would prevent the Legislature from changing rates (2/3 requirement is already needed for tax increases; but rate decreases could be done by majority? Actually under Prop 30/55 constitutional provisions, the rates are in the constitution, so amending requires 2/3 legislative or initiative. Under Prop 3 the same). Note: Under current law the rates already can't be changed without a ballot measure/2/3 legislative vote (since they're in the constitution). So making them permanent doesn't reduce flexibility much compared to now — the Legislature could amend the constitutional provisions with a 2/3 vote to let them sunset earlier or change rates. Wait, that's an important nuance: Article XIII Section 36(e)(f) is constitutional; the Legislature can amend a voter-approved constitutional provision only with 2/3 and voter approval. So the rates are already effectively locked in the constitution until 2030. Prop 3 removes the sunset. So future change requires either 2/3 legislature + majority voters, or an initiative. This is the same as today, just with a later date. So Skelton's concern ("tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters") is already true — they're embedded now. Prop 3 just extends the embedding indefinitely. So the incremental loss of flexibility is modest: currently, the sunset provides an automatic "release valve" in 2031 — voting no preserves that release valve.

That's actually the crux: the automatic expiration in 2031 is the one leverage point that forces the Legislature to engage in tax reform negotiation. If Prop 3 passes, that pressure disappears, and the status quo (volatile, top-heavy income tax + Prop 98 earmark) becomes permanent absent a future initiative.
