Blog Post · October 9, 2026
How Can Californians Make Sense of the Tax Measures on the November Ballot?
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Five of the fourteen statewide initiatives on the November ballot are tax measures. What implications might these initiatives have, and how are voters feeling about them? These questions were the focus of a lunchtime discussion last week in Sacramento.
Mark Baldassare, director of the PPIC Statewide Survey, kicked off the event with key insights from the most recent survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/).
The bottom line on the tax measures? “California voters are giving the five tax measures mixed reviews. Four of the five have majority support—but they’re not big majorities; they’re not over 60%. So the outcome is very uncertain.”
Baldassare pointed to other survey findings that could factor into ballot choices. “Most Californians say that there are too many initiatives on the ballot, and that the ballot initiatives are confusing,” he said. “The default is to vote no if you’re unsure.”
More broadly still, Baldassare noted that Californians are feeling negative about where things are heading in the state and the nation: “Majorities expect bad economic times over the next 12 months, and there are low approval ratings for elected leaders and low trust in the federal and state governments.”
Baldassare’s briefing set the stage for a discussion between Tani Cantil-Sakauye, PPIC president and CEO; Gale Kaufman, president of Kaufman Strategies; and Rob Stutzman, founder and president of Stutzman Public Affairs.
Cantil-Sakauye asked the panelists about how the overall mood might affect election outcomes. “It’s as bad as I can remember in terms of the negativity,” said Kaufman. However, she added that if past experience holds, voters will do their research on each of the ballot measures. “They pick each one individually,” she said. “You can’t make a blanket statement.”
Stutzman noted that voter negativity extends to both parties. “As much as you’re hearing about the midterms dynamic being driven by how unpopular the president is,” he said, “you still have a very unpopular Democratic Party.”
The tax measure that has attracted the most voter interest so far is Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Stutzman noted that the strongest argument for Prop 40 is that too much wealth has been accumulated by too few people. But Kaufman said that the measure has been divisive: “The Yes side of 40 has fragmented the Democratic coalition of activists throughout the state.” As Stutzman pointed out, disagreement about the potential impact of Prop 40 “allows the No campaign to point out that Becerra, Hilton, and Newsom are all opposed . . . and say this must be a bad idea.”
While Proposition 3—which would extend a temporary marginal tax on high-income Californians—had majority support in PPIC’s September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), less than half of voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 43, which would raise the vote threshold for approving local taxes to two-thirds.
For Stutzman, the relative lack of support for Prop 43 was a bit unexpected: “I was a little surprised when I saw the numbers,” he said. “But I also know that the would-be Yes side is preparing to spend money to push this over the top.” Kaufman said she was not surprised. “Making it more difficult for local entities to be able to tax themselves,” she said, “has a huge impact on cities, counties and special districts, who are really in trouble.”
In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”
***

Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

## State and Local Tax developments for the week of October 19, 2026
### Multistate: Voters to address several significant tax measures at the polls
**California**: The headline proposal is likely Proposition 40, an initiated measure that would impose a one-time five percent tax on California individual and fiduciary taxpayers with more than $1 billion in covered assets.
Covered assets would include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, but exclude real estate and qualified pension and retirement accounts.
Revenues from the proposal would be exempt from various spending limits.
Countering this measure is initiated Proposition 41, which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that exempt revenues from voter-approved spending limits.

Also on the ballot is Proposition 42, an initiated measure that would prohibit any new state tax imposed on the ownership of personal property or that applies retroactively based on a taxpayer’s past activities.
It would also nullify taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that conflict with the measure.
The California Constitution provides that if two or more conflicting measures are approved at the same election, the one receiving the greatest number of affirmative votes prevails.

Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Prop. 98 requires California to provide a minimum level of funding for K–12 schools and community colleges each year, based on state revenues, economic growth, and student enrollment. Local property taxes also contribute to the Prop. 98 minimum. Together, these requirements typically direct about 40% of General Fund revenues to education. 3
Of the education funding, 89% goes to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. None of the funding can be used for administrative costs. After meeting education requirements, revenues go to debt service and the rainy day fund; 50% of remaining funds, capped at $2 billion annually, may support Medi-Cal children’s and family health services.
Medi-Cal provides free or low-cost health care to nearly 15 million Californians. This funding is especially important after federal bill H.R. 1 made major cuts to health care and food assistance. Federal Medicaid cuts could cost Medi-Cal tens of billions of dollars annually and cause up to 2 million Californians to lose coverage.
Since January 1, 2012, the top-earner income tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, helping more than double school funding and support transitional kindergarten, expanded learning, free school meals, COVID-19 recovery, and teacher recruitment. 4 Before the passage of Prop. 30, California ranked 50th among states in per-student education spending. Now it ranks 16th (or 31st when accounting for the state’s cost of living). 5 However, because 80% of school spending goes to staff salaries and benefits, the state still has 22 students per teacher, compared with 15.4 nationally. 6
Recently, the tax has generated about $9 billion to $10 billion annually, although revenues fluctuate with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates annual revenues could range from $5 billion to $15 billion.
Notably, high earners have not fled the state because of this tax; California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade. 7 The state has lost less-educated and lower-income adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults because of affordability and cost-of-living concerns. 8
Californians for Protecting Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability led the effort to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, with funding from the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers. Some proponents oppose Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax, out of concern that it could undermine support for Prop. 3.
A citizen-initiated measure, Prop. 3 needs a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Allowing the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to expire would require major cuts to education spending on the next generation of Californians, which would disproportionately impact low-income children and students of color. This income tax revenue enabled California to become the first state offering free breakfast and lunch to all TK–12 students, plus free after-school programs prioritizing low-income neighborhoods.
California’s educational funding formula, the Local Control Funding Formula, directs the most resources to students who face the greatest educational hurdles, including grants for English learners, foster youth, homeless students, and low-income families in high-poverty districts. 9
Prop. 3 would backfill federal cuts and sustain up to $2 billion in annual funding for Medi-Cal, most of which goes to low-income people and people of color. Without state budget and policy intervention, the cuts from H.R. 1 are expected to completely destabilize California’s healthcare and hospital system, exacerbate food insecurity, and cause children to miss routine screenings and vaccines. 10
The measure is highly progressive; it does not increase taxes on couples earning less than $743,001 or individuals earning less than $341,001, in today’s dollars.
Pros
Prop. 3 would help backfill ongoing funding needs for children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal, which is facing severe federal funding cuts.
The measure would tax only California’s highest earners.
It would not increase the current income tax rate, which was set in 2012.
Any leftover capital-gains-driven revenue would lower state debt and help build the rainy day fund, which supports the state’s financial health and mitigates the volatility of this funding source.
There is no evidence that the tax has contributed to any significant tax flight from the state.
Because the tax is permanent, it would facilitate greater predictability in state revenues.
Cons
The state’s reliance on taxing the highest income earners would increase state budget volatility.
The measure is restrictive: it would require meeting the Prop. 98 education minimum before allowing flexibility in funding allocation.

Should Voters Approve Prop. 3? How Top Tax Rates Have Helped Californians
A Look at What California's Top Tax Rates Have Funded — and What's at Risk if Voters Don't Approve Prop. 3
July 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 3 will appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot, asking California voters whether to make permanent the higher-income tax rates on the state’s highest earners. These top tax rates were first enacted by voters in 2012 and renewed in 2016 to help fund schools, health care, and other supports for working families. Without action, the current rates are set to expire after 2030, reducing state revenues by billions of dollars annually and threatening funding for schools and state programs and services that support Californians every day.

What Would Prop. 3 Do?
Prop. 3 would make permanent the rates put in place since 2012, preserving a key element of progressivity (requiring households with higher incomes to pay higher tax rates) in the state’s revenue structure that funds critical investments that improve the quality of life for all Californians. The measure would not raise taxes or change existing income tax rates; it simply removes the expiration date on current tax rates for the state’s highest earners. Revenues would continue to support the entire state General Fund budget by helping meet the TK-14 constitutional funding guarantee and freeing up revenue for other programs and services, just as they have since 2012.
Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55
In 2012, after the state faced significant revenue losses as a result of the Great Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which added new income tax brackets for the state’s highest earners (10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3%, depending on household income) and included a temporary sales tax increase. Both the income tax rates and the sales tax increase were temporary, with the sales tax set to expire in 2016 and the income tax rates in 2018. Proposition 30 also created the Education Protection Account, a state account in the General Fund that receives and disburses revenues from the top income tax rates.
what is the education protection account (epa)?
Proposition 30 (2012) established the Education Protection Account, a state account where revenues from the top income tax rates are deposited. Of the funds in the account, 89% are distributed to schools and 11% to community colleges. This revenue is treated as General Fund revenue, subject to constitutional requirements including Prop. 98 (1988), the state’s minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education, and Prop. 2 (2014), which established rules for building state budget reserves and paying down state debts. The revenue deposited into the EPA increases the Prop. 98 guarantee and is used to help meet the guarantee, freeing up General Fund revenue for other state budget priorities.
In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended the income tax rates for another 12 years (to 2030), while allowing the sales tax to expire as scheduled. Prop. 55 also added a constitutional formula intended to increase funding for the Medi-Cal program (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3765) when revenues exceed a certain threshold. This specific formula has never directed funds to Medi-Cal, and the current measure would allow it to expire. However, top tax rate revenues do support the Medi-Cal budget indirectly through the General Fund capacity generated by Prop. 55.
Since their initial enactment in 2012, these higher tax rates have generated around $120 billion for schools and other essential services. In recent years, the higher rates have generated around $10 billion annually. These revenues now form a core component of the state budget, supporting the TK-14 education budget, strengthening General Fund capacity to support other vital programs and services, and building reserves.
Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?
The voter-approved top tax rates only impact the highest-income Californians.
These rates only apply to the top 2% of California tax filers (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016). In tax year 2025, these top rates only applied to people with incomes above around $371,000 for single tax filers and about $743,000 for married couples filing jointly. These thresholds increase annually with inflation.
Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Cut
The top-earning 1% of Californians would receive a major tax cut if Prop. 55 rates are not extended. If the voter-approved top tax rates are allowed to expire, the vast majority of tax filers in the top 1% by income would receive an average annual tax cut of nearly $59,000, according to estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. This top 1% group would get about 98% of the total tax cuts. The remaining tax cuts would go to some households in the next 4% of highest-income filers. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Not all households in the top 5% or top 1% would receive tax cuts from the expiration of the top tax rates for several reasons. First, filers are subject to the top tax rates if their taxable income — that is, income after accounting for allowed exemptions and deductions — exceeds the thresholds established by Prop. 30 and Prop. 50. In contrast, the thresholds for the top 5% and top 1% used by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for this analysis are based on total income before exemptions and deductions. So tax filers in the top 1% by total income may have taxable incomes under the threshold for the top rates. Second, some high-income filers that use specific tax preferences may be subject to an “alternative minimum tax,” which could be triggered if their regular tax bill were reduced. And finally, because thresholds for these rates vary by household type, a married couple filing a joint tax return with a total income of $500,000 falls into the top 5% of all tax filers, but their total income — even before accounting for exemptions and deductions — is below the threshold for the Prop. 55 taxes of around $743,000, for example. Around 15% of this group would receive a tax cut, averaging more than $2,000 annually. Californians in all other income groups would see no change to their taxes.
California’s tax system would be more regressive if the Prop. 55 tax rates expire. A regressive tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/) is one in which lower-income households pay larger shares of their income in taxes than higher-income households. In contrast, in a progressive tax system, higher-income people pay higher shares of their income in taxes. California’s tax system is more progressive than many other state tax systems (https://itep.org/whopays-7th-edition/), in large part due to these voter-approved top tax rates that are up for renewal under Prop. 3.
When you add up the various state and local taxes that Californians pay — including the sales tax, property tax, and other types of taxes — the highest-income 1% currently pay about 12% of their income in taxes on average. That’s barely more than the 11.7% paid by Californians in the lowest 20% by income. If the top rates were not in effect, the top 1% would pay only about 10.7% of their income in state and local taxes — lower than what the bottom fifth of Californians pay.
Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared
The number of Californians with incomes high enough to be subject to the voter-approved top tax rates has more than doubled, reflecting soaring incomes among top earners. Around 185,000 tax filers, including more than 175,000 California resident filers, had incomes above the thresholds for Prop. 30’s top tax rates in 2013, the first year the rates were in effect. By 2024 (the latest available data), the number had reached nearly 376,000, including around 355,000 California residents. 2 (javascript:void(0)) “Tax filer” represents a tax filing unit — the primary filer as well as any spouses and dependents included on the tax return. A tax filing unit can be an individual, a couple, or a family, and in some cases can include unrelated dependents. This increase is due to the incomes of these high-income households growing much faster than inflation over this period.
Californians subject to the top tax rates have seen their incomes grow dramatically over the past several decades, while most Californians have lost ground or experienced income declines after adjusting for inflation . The top 1% of Californians saw their inflation-adjusted incomes increase more than 2.5 times (157%) between 1987 and 2024, while those in the bottom 80% saw decreases in real income over that time.
To be in the top 1%, a tax filer had an income of at least $973,097 in 2024. On average, this group reported more than $3 million per tax return in 2024 — about 54 times the income of the middle fifth of Californians, who earned around $56,000 on average. In even starker contrast, the top 0.1% had an average income of over $15 million — 268 times that of the middle fifth of Californians. In other words, someone in the top 1% can earn in just under one week what the average middle-income Californian earns in an entire year, and someone in the top 0.1% can earn that amount in just over a day .
What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?
Since the passage of Prop. 30 in 2012, the top tax rates have generated about $120 billion in state revenue. 3 (javascript:void(0)) This figure reflects revenues from the top tax rates allocated to TK-14 education from the Education Protection Account (EPA) through the 2024-25 fiscal year. On average, this revenue has represented about 5.5% of total General Fund revenues. The funds raised by the top tax rates approved by voters through Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have been a major revenue source for the state, supporting critical services including education, health care, and economic security programs. This revenue has also helped the state to build up budget reserves to be better prepared for downturns when revenues decline or come in lower than expected.
The annual revenue raised by the top tax rates has increased in line with overall state revenues . These revenues are sensitive to stock market fluctuations, as a large share of the income of high-income households comes from earnings on investments such as dividends and capital gains. For example, Prop. 55 revenues peaked at more than $16 billion when the stock market surged in 2021 and then subsequently fell in line with the stock market decline in the following years, before growing to nearly $12 billion in 2024. The sensitivity of these revenues to economic conditions makes it all the more important that state leaders have the capacity to save revenues during high-revenue years in the state’s budget reserves for future downturns, as required under Prop. 2 of 2014 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/140924_Proposition_2_BB.pdf)— which may be modified to require additional savings in some strong-revenue years if voters approve changes to the existing measure with Prop. 2 on the November 2026 ballot.
Top tax rate revenues provide critical support for schools and community colleges . Top tax rate revenues serve two purposes for the TK-14 education budget: 1) increase the Prop. 98 minimum guarantee’s annual calculation and 2) provide the revenues needed to meet the guarantee. Because top tax rate revenues count as General Fund revenues, they directly affect how the annual Prop. 98 level is calculated. In years when the General Fund experiences strong growth, the guarantee is set as a share (about 40%) of General Fund revenues, establishing a higher floor. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The minimum guarantee is determined using one of three formulas: 1) approximately 40% of General Fund revenue, 2) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and growth in per capita personal income, or 3) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and per capita General Fund revenue growth. In other years, the guarantee builds on the prior year’s level, carrying forward the growth built when revenues were strong. Regardless of how the guarantee is calculated, the effect of the top tax rate revenue is cumulative. As shown in the chart below, the guarantee has grown on an ongoing basis since 2012-13, with part of this growth attributable to the top tax rates.
what is proposition 98?
Prop. 98 is a constitutional amendment adopted by California voters in 1988 that establishes an annual minimum funding level for TK-14 education each fiscal year, commonly referred to as the minimum guarantee. Prop. 98 funding comes from a combination of state General Fund revenue and local property taxes. Prop. 98 spending supports TK-12 schools, community colleges, county offices of education, the state preschool program, and state agencies that provide direct TK-14 instructional programs. While Prop. 98 establishes a required minimum funding level for programs falling under the guarantee as a whole, it does not protect individual programs from reduction or elimination.
In addition to raising the guarantee’s calculation, Prop. 55 revenues directly help meet the guarantee. Revenues from the top tax rates are used to meet the Prop. 98 obligation, which frees up General Fund dollars that would otherwise be needed to meet the guarantee. These freed-up dollars are used to support non-TK-14 programs, build state reserves, and pay down debts. Since 2012-13, when these revenues began to flow to schools and community colleges, Prop. 55 revenues have provided about $120 billion to help meet the TK-14 budget. 5 (javascript:void(0)) While the top tax rate revenues have provided approximately $120 billion to the TK-14 budget through the EPA, because these revenues also reduce the General Fund dollars to meet the guarantee, the overall education funding impact is approximately 40% of total revenues.
The chart below shows the growth in the minimum guarantee, and the share provided by the top tax rate revenues, adjusted to 2024 dollars. Throughout this period, top tax rate revenues have enabled the state to implement key educational programs. For example, in the 2013-14 school year, policymakers began implementing a major school finance reform (https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4108/download?inline&file=CA_LCFF_School_Funding_Effectiveness_REPORT.pdf) to more equitably allocate dollars to school districts based on student need.
Top tax rate revenues have also created more General Fund capacity to support critical economic security, housing, and health programs.

California’s Earned Income Tax Credit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/caleitc/) , which boosts incomes for workers who earn little from their jobs, was initially established in 2015, and was expanded to more Californians in 2017 and 2018.
In 2021, policymakers launched a multi-year plan to fund an increase of 200,000 child care slots, reaching about 152,000 in 2026-27, making progress in expanding access to children and families with low incomes.
In 2019, the state created the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) program, which provides funding to localities to finance solutions tailored to their needs and has shown positive outcomes, including reducing youth homelessness (https://jbay.org/resources/investing-in-impact-2025/) .
Policymakers restored several Medi-Cal benefits between 2014 and 2019 that had been cut due to budget shortfalls during the Great Recession, including adult dental benefits, podiatry, optometry, audiology, and speech therapy services .
The state has made progress on reducing deep poverty among families with children by increasing CalWORKs cash grants (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/the-role-of-calworks-in-alleviating-deep-poverty/) , and reducing poverty among older adults and people with disabilities by increasing Supplemental Security Income/State Supplementary Payment (SSI/SSP) grants (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/ssi-ssp-grants-moving-in-the-right-direction-but-still-not-enough/) , after both programs had been subject to deep cuts during the Great Recession.

4.1  The Prop 30 Baseline: Avoidance Dominated Migration 
Empirical analysis of Proposition 30 provides the most important baseline for the avoidance question: physical migration accounted for only approximately 9.5% of the total revenue erosion from that tax increase (Rauh & Shyu 2024).

Prop 3 doesn't change the rates — it just prevents a future decrease. If the rates fall in 2031, would income come back? Possibly partially, plus people who left might return. So the LAO's $5-15B may overstate the revenue that would actually be lost if rates expire... Actually, the LAO's estimate for the loss is likely based on current revenue from those brackets, which is real revenue actually collected now ($10-12B recently). So it's the actual current revenue. But there's an argument that a rate reduction could produce more revenue than the naive "windfall" symmetry implies — i.e., some income might come back. Conversely, if rates stay, there could be continued erosion over time. The LAO range of $5-15B accounts for volatility.

Let me now check the LA Times article "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" for the detail, plus the LAO's earlier initiative analysis (A.G. File 2025-016) for more nuance, and any analysis of what happens if it fails (whether the Legislature would replace it). Also, check campaign finance: how much was raised/spent on both sides (the no side appears underfunded).

Also I should consider the counterfactual: if Prop 3 fails, does the Legislature have to do something? Rates expire in 2031; the Legislature could act with a 2/3 vote, or voters could pass something in 2028/2030. So a "no" vote is not necessarily a permanent loss of revenue — but it creates a cliff and uncertainty, and the political economy makes restoration hard (a 2/3 legislative vote is unlikely; a future ballot measure is possible but not guaranteed).

Let me also consider: is there something problematic about the measure's drafting? E.g., it amends Article XIII Section 36 in full text — which also includes the 2011 realignment provisions. Also, the Medi-Cal formula in Prop 55 (subparagraph F) — the measure keeps it (50% of remainder up to $2B). Also, does Prop 3 remove the "Public School System Stabilization Account" provisions? No, it amends Section 36(e)(2) to remove the 2030 date limits presumably. Let me check the remaining text (offset 40000) to see the last part and any other amendments (e.g., whether the sunset removals are properly drafted, and whether Section 7 proponent standing etc.).

Actually, an important drafting question: does the measure delete the "inoperative on December 1, 2031" clauses? The text shown includes "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." — Wait, that appears in the text I fetched. Hmm, but the strikeout/italic formatting is lost in the plain text extraction. The LAO says Prop 3 removes the sunset. In the printed VIG, deleted text is in strikeout. The plain-text extraction shows both deleted and added text without formatting. So "(D) This paragraph shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031." is likely in strikeout (deleted). Let me verify with the LAO analysis PDF (lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) which includes Figure 1 and describes the proposal.

Let me also check the remaining chunk of the text (offset 40000) to see if there's anything else notable.

Then I'll consider the final decision. Let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
1. Not a new tax — maintains rates in place 15 years; avoids an abrupt $5-15B annual revenue cliff (2-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031.
2. Revenue supports Prop 98 education minimum and frees General Fund for Medi-Cal (facing federal cuts under H.R. 1), reserves, debt paydown.
3. Highly progressive: top 1% gets 98% of the tax cut if it expires (ITEP). Without the rates, the top 1% would pay a lower effective state/local tax share than the bottom 20% (per CBPC).
4. Accountability provisions: EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs; annual audits; criminal penalties for misuse; districts post accounting online. Local boards decide spending.
5. Migration evidence is mixed/weak: FTB measured outmigration at 0.1-0.2% of those subject to higher rate; CA has second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves; Young & Varner found near-zero millionaire migration elasticity.
6. Broad, mainstream support: CTA, PTA, school nurses, CMA (doctors), firefighters, Planned Parenthood, Cal Dem Party, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, SPUR, LA Times (no official board position but coverage). Polling shows ~54-58% support.
7. The alternative — a no vote — doesn't produce reform; it just risks a cliff. The "message vote" theory has a poor track record (Prop 55 in 2016 got rejected by Chronicle board expecting reform; none happened).

Arguments for NO:
1. "Temporary" becomes permanent — a broken promise; sets precedent.
2. Entrenches rates and earmarks in the Constitution, removing legislative flexibility; tax rates in the constitution can only be changed by voters (Skelton's point). Locks in Prop 98 + EPA earmark structure; makes comprehensive tax reform harder (e.g., broadening the base, reducing volatility).
3. Entrenches revenue volatility: half of state income tax from top 2%, tied to capital gains/stock market; Prop 98 minimum guarantee linked to volatile revenue → boom/bust cycles in school funding. LAO and Chronicle both flag this.
4. Behavioral responses: Rauh & Shyu find significant intensive-margin erosion; making the high rates permanent could increase incentives for long-run income shifting, and interacts with Prop 40 wealth tax and other measures (software tax, health insurance tax) raising the cumulative tax burden → competitiveness concerns; top rate 13.3% is highest in nation.
5. Cost-of-living/political-economy: 55% of Californians prefer lower taxes/fewer services; small-business pass-through burden (NFIB).
6. No reform attached: measure has no spending accountability for the ~60% that goes to non-education General Fund uses, despite campaign claims that "every dollar goes to schools." The LA Times fact-check shows the campaign framing overstates. Also, no education-outcome accountability (SDUT argument: spending up, outcomes flat).
7. There's time: rates don't expire until 2031; the Legislature/voters could revisit in 2028 or 2030 with reforms attached (e.g., a broadened base, spending reforms). A no vote creates leverage.

Counter to the "no rush" point: the campaign needs to happen well in advance of 2031 for budget planning; also CTA put it on the ballot now for a reason (midterm electorate more favorable? Actually, midterms are usually worse for tax measures — low turnout, more conservative electorate. Hmm, but polls show it passing).

Consider the risk asymmetry: If Prop 3 passes and later turns out that reform was needed, the rates can still be changed by a future ballot measure (majority vote) — the constitution can be amended by initiative. So permanence isn't irreversible: it just requires a ballot measure rather than a 2/3 legislative vote. That reduces the "lock-in" concern significantly. Indeed, if a majority of voters later wanted lower rates, they could pass an initiative to lower them (though initiative to lower taxes is straightforward—statutory or constitutional). So permanence is a moderate, not extreme, loss of flexibility.

If Prop 3 fails: a $5-15B hole (midpoint ~$10B, ~4% of General Fund) appears in 2031-32, requiring either deep cuts to schools/health care or a new tax measure or 2/3 legislative action (unlikely in the current political climate, and even more unlikely given anti-tax momentum). Also uncertainty harms multi-year budget planning, and the state currently faces structural deficits. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) starting to bite, and CA's structural deficit, losing $10B/year would force real cuts. CTA claims 15% school budget cut; that's probably overstated (the LAO says ~40% goes to education, so a $10B loss → ~$4-6B less for schools; Prop 98 guarantee would fall accordingly). Still significant.

Given the framing "yes or no" and my analysis, the balance favors YES: it maintains existing, broadly popular, highly progressive revenue; avoids a large fiscal cliff; includes real accountability provisions; the migration evidence is mixed and mostly points to modest effects; and the loss of flexibility is bounded because a future initiative can still change rates. The strongest counterarguments (entrenchment of volatility, broken "temporary" promise, no structural reform) are real but are second-order compared with a $5-15B annual revenue cliff during a period of federal health care cuts.

Let me do a couple more checks to be thorough:
- LAO PDF Figure 1 & proposal description (confirm sunset removal, and whether Prop 55's Medi-Cal formula is retained or allowed to expire).
- Campaign finance totals for both sides.
- Any notable "no" endorsements from unusual quarters (e.g., some Democrats like Gov. Newsom? Reform California? Also, does any progressive group oppose on grounds it forecloses a better deal?).
- Check the LA Times fact-check article details.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by
making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement

Very useful. Key facts:
- CTA spent ~$60M; total $81M for, $5,500 against (essentially no opposition campaign).
- Some billionaires (Building a Better California) endorse Prop 3 while fighting Prop 40.
- Gov. Newsom supports Prop 3 (per LA Times: "Others in that camp include ... Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra" — that camp being Yes on 3 and No on 40).

Let me now check a couple more things:
1. Any credible criticism from the left or good-government groups (e.g., League of Women Voters California position; Common Cause; California Forward).
2. What the LAO said in its initiative analysis (A.G. File 2025-016) — including any unusual notes, e.g., whether the measure would prevent the Legislature from changing rates (2/3 requirement is already needed for tax increases; but rate decreases could be done by majority? Actually under Prop 30/55 constitutional provisions, the rates are in the constitution, so amending requires 2/3 legislative or initiative. Under Prop 3 the same). Note: Under current law the rates already can't be changed without a ballot measure/2/3 legislative vote (since they're in the constitution). So making them permanent doesn't reduce flexibility much compared to now — the Legislature could amend the constitutional provisions with a 2/3 vote to let them sunset earlier or change rates. Wait, that's an important nuance: Article XIII Section 36(e)(f) is constitutional; the Legislature can amend a voter-approved constitutional provision only with 2/3 and voter approval. So the rates are already effectively locked in the constitution until 2030. Prop 3 removes the sunset. So future change requires either 2/3 legislature + majority voters, or an initiative. This is the same as today, just with a later date. So Skelton's concern ("tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters") is already true — they're embedded now. Prop 3 just extends the embedding indefinitely. So the incremental loss of flexibility is modest: currently, the sunset provides an automatic "release valve" in 2031 — voting no preserves that release valve.

That's actually the crux: the automatic expiration in 2031 is the one leverage point that forces the Legislature to engage in tax reform negotiation. If Prop 3 passes, that pressure disappears, and the status quo (volatile, top-heavy income tax + Prop 98 earmark) becomes permanent absent a future initiative.

3. Also check the state's structural deficit situation for 2026-27, LAO's fiscal outlook, to gauge the stakes. And whether a "no" vote would create a crisis in 2031 or whether the state could offset.

4. Check League of Women Voters California position and any other nonpartisan guides (e.g., California Forward, Silicon Valley Leadership Group).

Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed constitutional initiative that maintains personal income tax rates for high-income taxpayers (A.G. File No. 25-0016).
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Personal Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for the majority of spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Recent Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend This Money? The state collects taxes from people and businesses and uses them to pay for services to the public. This year, the state plans to spend about $230 billion from the General Fund. About half of this spending is for K-12 schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The amount spent on K-12 schools and community colleges is set by the State Constitution.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's health insurance program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, parole programs, and courts.
Proposal
This measure maintains the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 by making them permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Measure Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by this measure is hard to predict and will go up and down with the economy. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing investment income and capital gains. These types of income are closely tied to the stock market and therefore go up and down a lot from year to year. In a weak year, the measure might bring in around $5 billion in revenue. In a strong year, the measure might bring in $15 billion in annual revenue. In most years, revenue brought in by the measure would be in between these amounts. These amounts are in today's dollars and would tend to grow over time.
A Large Portion of the Money Would Go to Schools and Community Colleges. The State Constitution requires the state to spend a large portion of new money on schools and community colleges. Typically, about 40 percent of the revenue brought in by this measure would go to schools and community colleges.
A Smaller Portion of the Money Would Go to Reserves. The State Constitution requires the state to set aside money to save in budget reserves. Reserves help the state balance its budget when the economy is weak and revenues decline. Some of the money brought in under this measure would be saved in reserves. This means the state would have more money in savings to balance the budget when the economy is weak.
Remaining Money Could Be Spent on Other State Programs. Money brought in under this measure that does not go to schools, community colleges, or reserves could be used for other state programs.
Summary of Fiscal Effects. We estimate the measure would have the following major fiscal effects:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income taxes (in today's dollars) by making a tax on high income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

An income tax on California’s highest earners, first passed in 2012, will expire in five years unless voters make the levy for school funding permanent. Below, an anti-tax advocate argues California’s pattern of making temporary taxes permanent is bad policy, and voters can break the cycle. The opposing view: A cafeteria manager says students and families will be hit hardest (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) if Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) fails. Guest Commentary written by Robert Gutierrez Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association. For more than a century, California’s tax system has followed a familiar pattern: A fiscal crisis emerges, government responds with a “temporary” tax increase, the crisis passes and the tax remains. Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would continue this troubling pattern by making a “temporary” tax increase permanent. Supporters of Prop. 3 argue that the measure will provide ongoing funding for two priorities of most Californians, education and healthcare. The question is not whether those services matter — clearly, they do — but whether it is a sound policy to permanently extend tax hikes that voters were repeatedly told would expire. When California voters approved higher personal income tax rates in 2012, they were told the increase was a short-term emergency response to a specific fiscal challenge. Four years later, voters were asked to extend the tax increases, again for a limited time. Prop. 3 would make the tax hikes permanent — during a year in which high taxes and the unaffordable cost of living are the biggest problems for the majority of Californians. A recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) found that roughly half of Californians say the cost of living is their top concern, and 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer government services. The reason that “temporary” tax hikes rarely disappear is that once government adjusts its spending to the higher revenue, politicians and special interests treat this as the new baseline. It doesn’t have to be this way. By rejecting Prop. 3, California voters can break the tradition and make sure that a temporary tax truly is temporary. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Proposition 3 sustains California schools. Losing the high-income tax would be devastating (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) It is worth noting that California’s new state budget establishes record-high education spending of $27,418 per pupil (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/TK-12Education.pdf), up 27% from just five years earlier (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2021-22/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/K-12Education.pdf). Public schools continue to be the state’s top priority, receiving roughly 46% of the state’s general fund budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/SummaryCharts.pdf). Additionally, the entire budget reached a record high of $351.7 billion in spending, an $89 billion increase in spending (34%) from five years ago. In other words, any fiscal emergency of the past has been addressed. Supporters characterize Prop. 3 as affecting only high-income taxpayers, but it is not that simple. California’s tax system does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, reporting business earnings on personal income tax returns. As a result, extending higher tax rates would sustain higher costs for many small businesses — ultimately resulting in higher prices for their customers. The broader economic effects deserve scrutiny, as well. California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and has the highest state sales tax rate and gas tax. The state applies an additional 1.3% tax on all wage income to pay for the State Disability Insurance program. In addition to keeping costs high in California, Prop. 3 would deepen California’s reliance on the state’s most volatile revenue source: taxes paid by high-income earners (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/#5dfdd7c1-ccba-4770-802a-ec01052bfd71). During economic expansions, revenue surges. During downturns, revenue can fall dramatically, leaving the state struggling to pay ongoing expenses — especially when the demand for public services is increasing. Expanding permanent spending commitments tied to the most volatile revenue stream reduces flexibility when the economy weakens. Education and healthcare deserve stable funding. But stable funding should rest on honest budgeting and prioritizing the ample resources already available — not on repeatedly extending taxes that voters were assured would expire. This high-income tax was pitched as ‘temporary.’ California voters can ensure it stays that way

By Robert Gutierrez, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

An income tax on California's highest earners, first passed in 2012, will expire in five years unless voters make the levy for school funding permanent. Below, an anti-tax advocate argues California's pattern of making temporary taxes permanent is bad policy, and voters can break the cycle. The opposing view: A cafeteria manager says students and families will be hit hardest if Proposition 3 fails.

Guest Commentary written by

For more than a century, California’s tax system has followed a familiar pattern: A fiscal crisis emerges, government responds with a “temporary” tax increase, the crisis passes and the tax remains.

Proposition 3 would continue this troubling pattern by making a “temporary” tax increase permanent.

Supporters of Prop. 3 argue that the measure will provide ongoing funding for two priorities of most Californians, education and healthcare. The question is not whether those services matter — clearly, they do — but whether it is a sound policy to permanently extend tax hikes that voters were repeatedly told would expire.

When California voters approved higher personal income tax rates in 2012, they were told the increase was a short-term emergency response to a specific fiscal challenge. Four years later, voters were asked to extend the tax increases, again for a limited time.

Prop. 3 would make the tax hikes permanent — during a year in which high taxes and the unaffordable cost of living are the biggest problems for the majority of Californians. A recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California found that roughly half of Californians say the cost of living is their top concern, and 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer government services.

The reason that “temporary” tax hikes rarely disappear is that once government adjusts its spending to the higher revenue, politicians and special interests treat this as the new baseline.

It doesn’t have to be this way. By rejecting Prop. 3, California voters can break the tradition and make sure that a temporary tax truly is temporary.

And the pro case: SPUR, LWV, CBPC, Chronicle, LA Times (no board position but coverage), Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, Daily Bruin.

Now let me consider the empirical balance more carefully.

1. Revenue at stake: $5-15B/yr, most years ~$10B. That's ~4% of the $250B General Fund. If lost in 2031, Prop 98's guarantee would fall (about 40% → ~$4B less for schools; though actually the LAO notes the guarantee's calculation depends on formula; schools could lose more over time due to cumulative effects). Rest is General Fund for Medi-Cal etc., at a time when the state has $20-35B structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts.

2. Does a no vote really force reform? History: In 2016, Chronicle board hoped rejecting Prop 55 would force reform; it passed anyway and no reform happened. The realistic counterfactual if Prop 3 fails is not "comprehensive tax reform" but "state budget crisis in 2031 and a scramble." Also, if it fails, CTA has two more chances (2028, 2030) to put it back on the ballot — meaning a no vote likely just delays, and the delay creates budget uncertainty (districts hold back reserves earlier, per Goldberg).

3. Who bears the tax? Top 2% of filers, ~376,000 filers (355,000 residents). Top 1% would get 98% of the tax cut if it expires (ITEP: avg ~$59,000/yr). Effective state+local tax rate of top 1% (12%) vs bottom 20% (11.7%) — without the rates, the top 1% would pay 10.7%, less than the bottom fifth. That's a strong equity argument for YES.

4. Migration/behavioral response: Rauh & Shyu find real responses (0.8pp extra outmigration of top bracket; elasticity 2.5-3.2; ~45-61% of windfall eroded). But (a) that erosion has already occurred and is embedded in the current ~$10B revenue; (b) FTB measured outmigration at 0.1-0.2% of affected taxpayers; (c) CBPP: state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves; (d) Young & Varner found near-zero millionaire migration elasticity for the 1991 Prop (CA's millionaire tax); (e) SPUR notes CA has second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households over the past decade; PPIC finds those leaving CA are disproportionately lower-income/less-educated, driven by housing costs, not income taxes. So the migration argument against Prop 3 is empirically weak-to-moderate; the intensive margin (income shifting/reduced income generation) is a more credible concern, but again already priced into actual revenues.

Also note the counter-consideration: if Prop 3 fails and rates drop in 2031, the revenue "windfall" of the cut could be partially offset by income returning — so the loss may be less than $5-15B; but symmetric logic suggests the LAO estimate is reasonable.

5. Volatility concern: real. California's PIT is heavily top-weighted and capital-gains-linked; the LAO warns about stock-market risk. Prop 3 entrenches this. But note Prop 3's structure sends excess revenue to reserves (Prop 2) and the rainy day fund, which mitigates. Also Prop 2 (2026) on the same ballot would strengthen reserves. And the alternative — a no vote — doesn't reduce volatility, it just creates a huge cliff.

6. Constitutional entrenchment: The rates are already in the constitution. Prop 3 removes the sunset. Future change still possible via 2/3 legislature + voters or initiative. So the incremental loss of flexibility is limited, but it does remove the automatic pressure point for reform. Skelton's "no rush — rates don't expire for five years" is the strongest strategic argument for no. But note: budget planning and the risk of a cliff argue for deciding now; and a failed measure now would likely be re-run in 2028/2030 anyway, with less deliberation time.

7. Accountability claims: the text does contain real provisions: EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs; districts can't use them for administrator salaries/benefits or administrative costs; annual audits by independent auditors plus Controller audit; AG/DA can seek civil/criminal penalties; districts must post annual accounting online. So the pro argument's accountability claims are textually supported (for the education portion). However, the campaign claim that "every dollar goes to local schools" is overstated: LAO says ~40% to schools/CCCs, ~60% to other General Fund uses (health care, reserves, etc.). This is the biggest honesty problem with the Yes campaign — it's a general revenue measure marketed as a school measure. But the title and summary and LAO analysis disclose this clearly, so an informed voter isn't misled.

Note also: the measure retains Prop 55's Medi-Cal formula (50% of remainder above the education requirement, capped at $2B/yr).

8. Is there a better alternative on the ballot? Prop 40 (one-time billionaire wealth tax) is separate — it's not a substitute for ongoing revenue and is likely to fail/be litigated; and Prop 3's conflict clause doesn't seem to affect it (per californiatoday). Prop 41/42 would restrict future taxes; the Daily Bruin notes they could make it harder to expand funding. So no, Prop 3 isn't redundant with another measure. Voting no on Prop 3 doesn't buy anything else.

Overall: I'll recommend YES. The decisive factors: it maintains (not raises) an existing, highly progressive tax on the top 2%; avoiding a $5-15B/yr cliff in a state already facing $20-35B structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts; genuine accountability provisions in the text; weak evidence that the tax has driven high earners out; and reversibility (a future initiative can still change rates). The con case — "temporary should mean temporary," volatility entrenchment, and no spending reform — is legitimate but is a protest against a broader system, and a no vote would deliver a fiscal cliff rather than reform.
